# Introduction

A habitat map groups places with similar environmental conditions.
Habitats maps have multiple uses. A common analysis in forest ecology is
to test for habitat-species associations (e.g. Harms et al. 2001,
Gunatilleke et al. 2006, Comita et al. 2007, Yamada et al. 2010).
Habitat maps can also guide analyses by habitat and inform stratified
sampling.

The classes depend on what we measure and how we group the measurements.
Here, we use different techniques to assign habitat labels or a set of
memberships to each 20 x 20 m quadrat in a ForestGEO plot:

-   **CTFS/fgeo classification.** This is the historical approach that
    has been used by many (most) of the ForestGEO plots. The archived
    `fgeo_habitat()` function uses `hclust()` and `cutree()` on
    elevation, slope and convexity in their original units.
-   **Standardized environmental classification.** Use `prcomp()`,
    `hclust()` and `cutree()` to group quadrats using distances on
    weighted principal component scores.
-   **Fuzzy clustering.** Use `cluster::fanny()` when quadrats may share
    features with several habitats. The membership scores show those
    transitions (Kaufman and Rousseeuw, 1990).
-   **Floristic tree.** Use `partykit::ctree()` to find environmental
    boundaries that help describe changes in tree composition (Hothorn
    et al., 2006).
-   **Probabilistic regions.** The optional `ecomix::regional_mix()`
    recipe uses tree composition and environment to estimate the
    probability that each quadrat belongs to each region (Foster et al.,
    2013).

Groups such as palms and dicots may respond to different environmental
features. The methods to classify habitats may be applied independently
to different subsets of the individuals. This remains the user's
responsibiilty: this tutorial does not develop tools to split the
individuals/species into groups in a consistent or testable way. (Drop
me a line if you want to do so, it seems an interesting problem...).\
\
After fitting the maps, the tutorial shows how to inspect one habitat
map, smooth its boundaries, find indicator species and assess
species--habitat associations. These analyses, in turn, can guide
choices such as the number of habitats and other parameters.

# Data and shared objects {#sec-preparation}

## Set up the example

We use data from the 50-ha Barro Colorado Island (BCI) plot in Panama.
All three files are in `data_examples/`. See the [dataset
notes](../../data_examples/README.md).

-   **`census1.txt`** is the historical first census export, nominally
    1982, with measurements from 1981--1983. Credit goes to the BCI
    census team, including Stephen P. Hubbell, Robin B. Foster, Richard
    Condit and collaborators, and Smithsonian/ForestGEO.
-   **`bci-elevation.csv`** contains 20,301 elevation locations on a 5 m
    grid. Its values match `BCIelev.tsv` in the CC0 archive (Condit et
    al., 2019).
-   **`bci-soils-wolf-2015.csv`** contains the complete 2010 soil survey
    of 625 locations, including local and UTM coordinates and 24 soil
    variables (Wolf et al., 2015). [Publisher's CC0
    deposit](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.3562863).

Run from the repository root or the tutorial folder. Set `path.to.fgeo2`
when working elsewhere. With your own prepared data, run the setup and
continue at the method you want to use.

```{r}
#| label: habitat-setup

path.to.fgeo2 = if(file.exists("../../fgeo2.Rproj")) "../.." else "."
# path.to.fgeo2 = "/full/path/to/fgeo2"

census.file = "census1.txt"
soil.file = "bci-soils-wolf-2015.csv"
plot.extent = c(0, 1000, 0, 500)  # xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax in metres.
quadrat.size = 20

# Install the packages for the recipes you want to run.
# install.packages(c("terra", "interp", "FNN", "cluster", "partykit",
#                    "indicspecies", "withr", "jsonlite"))

input.dir <- file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "data_examples")
source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "03_spatial/R/new/quadrats.R"))
source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2,
	"06_topography_habitat/R/new/topography-variables.R"))
```

## Define the population

Count living trees at least 1 cm in diameter. Each `TreeID` is
represented by its largest stem. This keeps trees with multiple stems
from entering the count more than once.

```{r}
#| label: habitat-individuals

minimum.dbh.cm = 1
living.status = "alive"

# Keep IDs as text. Diameter in this file is in millimetres.
census <- read.delim(file.path(input.dir, census.file),
	colClasses = c(TreeID = "character", StemID = "character"))

dbh.cm <- census$DBH / 10

keep <- census$Status %in% living.status &
	is.finite(dbh.cm) & dbh.cm >= minimum.dbh.cm &
	is.finite(census$PX) & is.finite(census$PY) &
	!is.na(census$Mnemonic) & nzchar(census$Mnemonic)

eligible <- census[keep, ]
eligible <- eligible[order(eligible$TreeID, -eligible$DBH, eligible$StemID), ]
eligible <- eligible[!duplicated(eligible$TreeID), ]

individuals <- data.frame(
	individual_id = eligible$TreeID,
	x = eligible$PX, y = eligible$PY,
	species = eligible$Mnemonic, dbh_cm = eligible$DBH / 10
)

stopifnot(!anyNA(individuals$individual_id), !anyDuplicated(individuals$individual_id))

c(individuals = nrow(individuals), species = length(unique(individuals$species)))
```

## Make the quadrat-by-species matrix

The row names of `composition` are quadrat IDs. The columns are species
codes and the entries are numbers of individuals.

```{r}
#| label: habitat-composition

# Give the whole plot a grid, including quadrats with no eligible trees.
quadrats <- make_quadrats_fast(
	outer.xmin = plot.extent[1], outer.xmax = plot.extent[2],
	outer.ymin = plot.extent[3], outer.ymax = plot.extent[4],
	quadrat.side.x = quadrat.size, quadrat.side.y = quadrat.size
)

membership <- assign_points_to_quadrats(
	outer.x = individuals$x, outer.y = individuals$y,
	point.id = individuals$individual_id, quadrat.locations = quadrats,
	boundary.rule = "left_bottom"
)

stopifnot(identical(membership$point_id, individuals$individual_id),
	!anyNA(membership$quadrat_id))
individuals$quadrat_id <- membership$quadrat_id

composition <- unclass(table(
	factor(individuals$quadrat_id, levels = quadrats$quadrat_id),
	factor(individuals$species)
))

stopifnot(sum(composition) == nrow(individuals))
dim(composition)
```

## Match the environmental table

First, we leverage all the topographical variables available through
`derive_topography()`. See the [topography
tutorial](derive-topographical-variables.qmd).

```{r}
#| label: habitat-environment
whitebox::install_whitebox()

terrain.resolution = 5
fill.missing = TRUE

xyz <- read.csv(file.path(input.dir, "bci-elevation.csv"))

terrain <- derive_topography(
	xyz = xyz,
	resolution = terrain.resolution,
	extent = plot.extent,
	crs = "local",
	fill.missing = fill.missing
)

# Aggregate the fine grid to the same 20 m cells as the quadrat table.
stopifnot(quadrat.size %% terrain.resolution == 0)
terrain.quadrats <- terra::aggregate(terrain,
	fact = quadrat.size / terrain.resolution, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)

quadrat.xy <- cbind(
	x = (quadrats$xmin + quadrats$xmax) / 2,
	y = (quadrats$ymin + quadrats$ymax) / 2
)

environment <- as.data.frame(terra::extract(terrain.quadrats, quadrat.xy))
rownames(environment) <- quadrats$quadrat_id
```

Estimate soil values at the quadrat centres by inverse-distance
weighting (IDW), using the settings from the [environmental extraction
tutorial](environmental-extraction.qmd). We keep estimates just outside
the sampling hull where enough nearby observations are available. This
lets the torus test use the full rectangular grid.

```{r}
#| label: habitat-soil

soil.search.radius = 60  # Metres.
soil.power = 2
minimum.soil.neighbours = 3L
maximum.soil.neighbours = 12L

soils <- read.csv(file.path(input.dir, soil.file), check.names = FALSE)
names(soils) <- trimws(names(soils))
soil.columns <- setdiff(names(soils), c("uid", "qid", "gx", "gy", "utm_e", "utm_n"))

# Use the terrain quadrat grid and keep only observed values for each assay.
for(variable in soil.columns)
{
	keep <- is.finite(soils$gx) & is.finite(soils$gy) & is.finite(soils[[variable]])
	
	measurements <- as.matrix(soils[keep, c("gx", "gy", variable)])
	
	soil.layer <- terra::interpIDW(terrain.quadrats[[1]], measurements,
		radius = soil.search.radius, power = soil.power,
		minPoints = minimum.soil.neighbours, maxPoints = maximum.soil.neighbours)

	# Extraction at the centres follows quadrat order.
	environment[[paste0("soil_", variable)]] <- terra::extract(soil.layer, quadrat.xy)[[1]]
	
}

stopifnot(identical(rownames(environment), rownames(composition)),
	all(is.finite(as.matrix(environment))))
```

Join other layers, such as canopy or disturbance, by quadrat ID. Keep
`environment` and `composition` in the order of `quadrats$quadrat_id`.
Keep the coordinates and species in `individuals` for the torus
analysis. Use the same counting rules and grid to compare censuses on a
fixed map.

## Prepare environmental distances {#sec-environment-distances}

Scale the variables to unit variance and use principal component
analysis (PCA) to form uncorrelated axes. The full set of unweighted PC
scores preserves Euclidean distances in the scaled variables. Here we
multiply each score by its share of explained variance raised to the
power `0.25`, giving the main gradients extra weight. Set the power to
`0` for the original scaled distances. Several related measurements can
give one gradient more influence. Choose columns for your question and
check [soil measurement
quality](https://esapubs.org/archive/ecol/E096/204/metadata.php).

```{r}
#| label: environment-pca

# Parameter to give weights to PCs
pc.weight.power = 0.25

# # Use all variables, or select columns here.
# Exclude aspect_deg from the averaging and PCA because the arithmetic mean of 359° and 1° is 180°, even though both face north.
environment.columns <- names(environment)
if("aspect_deg" %in% environment.columns)
  environment.columns <- environment.columns[environment.columns != "aspect_deg"]

environment.selected <- environment[, environment.columns, drop = FALSE]

# Obtain a weighted PCA-based space:
environment.pca <- prcomp(environment.selected, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
variance.share <- environment.pca$sdev^2 / sum(environment.pca$sdev^2)
pc.weights <- variance.share^pc.weight.power
environment.pc.weighted <- environment.pca$x # initialize

for(j in seq_along(pc.weights))
	environment.pc.weighted[, j] <- environment.pc.weighted[, j] * pc.weights[j]

# Environmental distances in the rescaled environmental space:
environment.distance <- dist(environment.pc.weighted)
```

# Environment-only classifications

## CTFS/fgeo classification of topography {#sec-legacy}

`fgeo.analyze::fgeo_habitat()` calculates mean elevation, convexity and
slope. It then uses Euclidean distance, complete linkage and a fixed
number of classes. This is the historical/legacy approach used by many
ForestGEO sites and remains the most direct way of splitting plots into
habitats based on {x, y, z} data only.

The first chunk loads the archived CTFS terrain calculation and the
archived fgeo clustering step. The second shows the equivalent base R
clustering, using the same variables and number of classes.

```{r}
#| label: legacy-topography-inputs
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Load the archived CTFS and fgeo code"

ctfs.commit = "0a2c01dd560daacba0fdc2eb8c9280e2b9d2ea9d"
fgeo.commit = "d69bfe711263305fcbaf322d402eba2f1edfb084"

source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "evaluation/0-code-to-source.r"))
legacy <- new.env()

load_github_snapshot(commit = ctfs.commit, envir = legacy,
	scripts = c("evaluation/Condit/spatial/quadfunc.r",
		"evaluation/Condit/topography/slope.r"))

load_github_snapshot(repo = "forestgeo/fgeo.analyze", commit = fgeo.commit,
	scripts = "R/add_cluster.R", envir = legacy)

legacy.xyz <- xyz[order(xyz$x, xyz$y), ]
names(legacy.xyz)[names(legacy.xyz) == "z"] <- "elev"
plot.dimensions <- c(diff(plot.extent[1:2]), diff(plot.extent[3:4]))

legacy.metrics <- legacy$allquadratslopes(list(col = legacy.xyz),
	gridsize = quadrat.size, plotdim = plot.dimensions, edgecorrect = TRUE)

legacy.metrics <- legacy.metrics[, c("meanelev", "convex", "slope")]

# Confirm that each row describes the same quadrat as in the new grid.
xyz.keys <- paste(xyz$x, xyz$y)
corners <- cbind(
	xyz$z[match(paste(quadrats$xmin, quadrats$ymin), xyz.keys)],
	xyz$z[match(paste(quadrats$xmin, quadrats$ymax), xyz.keys)],
	xyz$z[match(paste(quadrats$xmax, quadrats$ymin), xyz.keys)],
	xyz$z[match(paste(quadrats$xmax, quadrats$ymax), xyz.keys)]
)

stopifnot(nrow(legacy.metrics) == nrow(quadrats),
	all(abs(legacy.metrics$meanelev - rowMeans(corners)) < 1e-7))
rownames(legacy.metrics) <- quadrats$quadrat_id
```

```{r}
#| label: legacy-habitat-clustering

habitat.k = 4L

raw.tree <- hclust(dist(legacy.metrics), method = "complete")
habitat.raw <- cutree(raw.tree, k = habitat.k)

# Check the result against the archived fgeo clustering step.
legacy.input <- structure(legacy.metrics, class = c("fgeo_topography", "data.frame"))
legacy.result <- legacy$add_cluster(legacy.input, n = habitat.k)
stopifnot(identical(unname(habitat.raw), legacy.result$cluster))

table(habitat.raw)
```

If you have the legacy package installed, you can also call
`fgeo.analyze::fgeo_habitat()` with
`list(col = legacy.xyz, xdim = 1000, ydim = 500)`, `gridsize = 20`,
`n = habitat.k` and `edgecorrect = TRUE`.

## Standardized environmental classification

If one has more than the elevation profile, it is reasonable/advisable
to use more (even all) environmental variables. This section shows how
to cluster the quadrats using the [weighted PCA
distances](#sec-environment-distances) from terrain and soil.

The following example tries several values of `k` (= the number of
habitats) before choosing the level of detail. Silhouette width compares
how close a quadrat is to its own group and to the nearest alternative
group. Higher values indicate clearer separation in the chosen
environmental variables. Inspect the smallest habitat and its location
before choosing a value of `k` --- often, marginal habitats pop up in
this type of automated analyses (for example, due to large gaps) and it
would be appropriate to merge with surrounding areas.

```{r}
#| label: standardized-environmental-classification

candidate.k = 2:6
habitat.k = NULL  # Supply a k from the table to choose it yourself.
minimum.class.quadrats = 10L
linkage = "ward.D2"

cluster.tree <- hclust(environment.distance, method = linkage)

cluster.diagnostics <- data.frame(k = candidate.k, silhouette = NA_real_,
	smallest.class = NA_integer_)

for(j in seq_along(candidate.k))
{
	groups <- cutree(cluster.tree, k = candidate.k[j])
	widths <- cluster::silhouette(groups, environment.distance)

	cluster.diagnostics$silhouette[j] <- mean(widths[, "sil_width"])
	cluster.diagnostics$smallest.class[j] <- min(table(groups))
}

# Choose the best silhouette among partitions with large enough classes.
eligible <- subset(cluster.diagnostics, smallest.class >= minimum.class.quadrats)

if(nrow(eligible) == 0)
	stop("No candidate k meets minimum.class.quadrats.")

if(is.null(habitat.k))
	habitat.k <- eligible$k[which.max(eligible$silhouette)]

stopifnot(habitat.k %in% eligible$k)

habitat.hclust <- cutree(cluster.tree, k = habitat.k)
cluster.diagnostics
table(habitat.hclust)
```

## Fuzzy environmental classes with FANNY {#sec-fanny}

FANNY can use a distance matrix directly. Pass the same weighted PCA
distances to compare fuzzy and hard classifications in the same space.
Each quadrat has membership scores that sum to one. The largest score
gives its hard label. Keep the full matrix to see gradual boundaries.

```{r}
#| label: fuzzy-environmental-habitats

habitat.k = 2L
membership.exponent = 1.5  # Higher values make memberships more similar.

fuzzy.fit <- cluster::fanny(environment.distance, k = habitat.k, diss = TRUE,
	memb.exp = membership.exponent, maxit = 500, tol = 1e-8)

habitat.fanny <- setNames(fuzzy.fit$clustering, rownames(environment))
membership.fanny <- fuzzy.fit$membership
rownames(membership.fanny) <- rownames(environment)

fuzzy.fit$convergence
table(habitat.fanny)
summary(apply(membership.fanny, 1, max))
```

Check convergence and the number of hard habitats. If memberships are
nearly equal everywhere or some hard classes disappear, try a lower
`membership.exponent` or a smaller `habitat.k`.

# Floristically-informed classifications

These techniques use floristic composition to find environmental
differences that matter for the sampled community. Choose composition
data that match your ecological question.

## Conditional inference tree {#sec-ctree}

A tree splits the quadrats into groups by environmental rules, such as
an elevation threshold. Multivariate regression trees use this idea
(De'ath, 2002). Here `ctree()` uses conditional tests to choose
variables and splits (Hothorn et al., 2006). Use the original soil and
terrain columns to keep the thresholds in their measured units. The
number of habitats follows from the stopping rule and tree size limits.

```{r}
#| label: floristically-informed-tree
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

tree.columns = names(environment)
minimum.occupied.quadrats = 10L
minimum.node.size = 50L
maximum.depth = 3L
split.criterion = 0.99
test.statistic = "quadratic"
split.statistic = "maximum"
tree.seed = 20261120

stopifnot(identical(rownames(environment), rownames(composition)))
species.keep <- colSums(composition > 0) >= minimum.occupied.quadrats
community <- composition[, species.keep, drop = FALSE]
training.rows <- rowSums(community) > 0

stopifnot(ncol(community) >= 2, any(training.rows))

# Hellinger transformation of the retained species' relative abundances.
community <- community[training.rows, , drop = FALSE]
community.hel <- sqrt(community / rowSums(community))
environment.tree <- environment[, tree.columns, drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(all(is.finite(as.matrix(environment.tree))))

# Join response and predictor columns and build the native tree formula.
floristic.data <- data.frame(community.hel, environment.tree[training.rows, , drop = FALSE])
response.names <- names(floristic.data)[seq_len(ncol(community.hel))]
predictor.names <- tail(names(floristic.data), ncol(environment.tree))
floristic.formula <- reformulate(predictor.names,
	response = paste(response.names, collapse = " + "))

set.seed(tree.seed)
floristic.tree <- partykit::ctree(floristic.formula, data = floristic.data,
	control = partykit::ctree_control(
		teststat = test.statistic, splitstat = split.statistic,
		mincriterion = split.criterion,
		minbucket = minimum.node.size, minsplit = 2L * minimum.node.size,
		maxdepth = maximum.depth
	))

# Assign each quadrat to a terminal node using its environmental values.
names(environment.tree) <- predictor.names
habitat.ctree <- predict(floristic.tree, newdata = environment.tree, type = "node")
names(habitat.ctree) <- rownames(environment)

table(habitat.ctree)
plot(floristic.tree, type = "simple")
```

The Hellinger transformation takes the square root of the proportion of
each species in a quadrat, here among the retained species (Legendre and
Gallagher, 2001). The tree uses differences in relative composition. A
quadrat with no retained trees can still receive a label from its
environmental values. The split tests guide the fit. Check predictions
with held-out spatial blocks if you need evidence that the rules work at
new locations (Roberts et al., 2017).

## Optional probabilistic regions {#sec-rcp}

Regions of Common Profile use a mixture model to relate composition to
environment (Foster et al., 2013). For each quadrat, `postProbs` uses
both the observed flora and environment. `predict()` gives probabilities
based on the environment alone, using a model fitted with the flora. The
model uses predictors directly. Here we use a small set of scaled
terrain and soil variables.

This optional chunk uses the GitHub package `ecomix`. It was checked on
simulated data. Fitting the full BCI data can take time. [Package
example](https://skiptoniam.github.io/ecomix/articles/RCP-example.html).

```{r}
#| label: optional-rcp-habitats
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true

rcp.columns = c("elevation_m", "slope_deg", "tpi_m", "soil_M3P", "soil_M3Ca")
minimum.occupied.quadrats = 10L
candidate.k = 2:4
number.starts = 10L
seed = 20261120

# remotes::install_github("skiptoniam/ecomix@17418626")
library(ecomix)
set.seed(seed)

rcp.environment <- as.data.frame(scale(environment[, rcp.columns, drop = FALSE]))

species.keep <- colSums(composition > 0) >= minimum.occupied.quadrats
rcp.data <- make_mixture_data(
	species_data = composition[, species.keep, drop = FALSE],
	covariate_data = rcp.environment
)

# The constructor puts species columns first and environmental columns last.
response.names <- names(rcp.data)[seq_len(sum(species.keep))]
predictor.names <- tail(names(rcp.data), ncol(rcp.environment))
names(rcp.environment) <- predictor.names
rcp.formula <- reformulate(predictor.names,
	response = paste0("cbind(", paste(response.names, collapse = ", "), ")"))

rcp.fits <- vector("list", length(candidate.k))

for(j in seq_along(candidate.k))
{
	starts <- regional_mix.multifit(
		rcp_formula = rcp.formula, species_formula = ~1,
		data = rcp.data, nRCP = candidate.k[j], family = "negative.binomial",
		nstart = number.starts, mc.cores = 1, titbits = TRUE
	)

	log.likelihood <- sapply(starts$multiple_fits, function(x)
		if(x$conv == 0) x$logl else -Inf)
	if(!any(is.finite(log.likelihood)))
		stop("No converged RCP start at k = ", candidate.k[j])

	rcp.fits[[j]] <- starts$multiple_fits[[which.max(log.likelihood)]]
}

rcp.diagnostics <- data.frame(k = candidate.k, BIC = sapply(rcp.fits, BIC))
regional.fit <- rcp.fits[[which.min(rcp.diagnostics$BIC)]]
rcp.diagnostics

posterior.rcp <- regional.fit$postProbs
prediction.rcp <- predict(regional.fit, newdata = rcp.environment)
rownames(posterior.rcp) <- rownames(prediction.rcp) <- rownames(environment)
habitat.rcp <- setNames(max.col(posterior.rcp, ties.method = "first"), rownames(environment))
```

Check that several starts give similar fits before using BIC to choose
the number of regions. Use the probabilities to describe gradual changes
in membership or use `habitat.rcp` for one label per quadrat.

# Spatial smoothing {#sec-smoothing}

Nearby quadrats often have similar conditions. Smoothing can reduce
isolated cells and make larger patches more contiguous and easier to see
and interpret ecologically and in the field. However, spatial smoothing
can also remove real features. For example, a stream habitat one quadrat
wide can disappear when most neighbouring quadrats belong to the
surrounding forest. Compare raw and smoothed maps, and think about
whether they are realistic and useful, before choosing which one to use.

Choose a map in the first line below. The rest of the tutorial evaluates
this one map. To compare alternative maps, repeat these sections for
each one using the same quadrats and species data. Class sizes,
environmental profiles and indicator species can help you choose a
useful number of habitats. Choose your map before using species data to
test associations with it.

```{r}
#| label: choose-habitat-map

habitats <- habitat.hclust
# habitats <- habitat.raw
# habitats <- habitat.fanny
# habitats <- habitat.ctree
# habitats <- habitat.rcp  # If you ran the optional recipe.
use.smoothed.map = FALSE  # Set TRUE to use the filtered map below.

stopifnot(identical(names(habitats), quadrats$quadrat_id),
	identical(names(habitats), rownames(composition)), !anyNA(habitats))

habitats.original <- habitats
```

The filter uses each quadrat and the eight neighbours in its 3 × 3
window. It replaces the habitat with the most common label in that
window. At the edge of the plot, it uses the cells within the plot. When
several labels are equally common, the quadrat keeps its original label.
All windows use the original map.

```{r}
#| label: smooth-habitat-map
#| fig-height: 5.5

# Put the habitat labels on the 20 m grid, using quadrat centres for alignment.
habitat.grid <- terra::rast(terra::ext(plot.extent),
	resolution = quadrat.size, crs = "")
quadrat.xy <- cbind(x = (quadrats$xmin + quadrats$xmax) / 2,
	y = (quadrats$ymin + quadrats$ymax) / 2)
quadrat.cells <- terra::cellFromXY(habitat.grid, quadrat.xy)

stopifnot(length(quadrat.cells) == terra::ncell(habitat.grid),
	!anyNA(quadrat.cells), !anyDuplicated(quadrat.cells),
	isTRUE(all.equal(quadrat.xy, terra::xyFromCell(habitat.grid, quadrat.cells))))

habitat.labels <- levels(factor(habitats.original))
habitat.key <- data.frame(code = seq_along(habitat.labels),
	habitat = habitat.labels)
original.codes <- integer(terra::ncell(habitat.grid))
original.codes[quadrat.cells] <- match(habitats.original, habitat.labels)
terra::values(habitat.grid) <- original.codes

# Each row gives the labels in one window. tabulate() skips NA at the edges.
windows <- terra::focalValues(habitat.grid, w = 3)
smoothed.codes <- original.codes

for(i in seq_len(nrow(windows)))
{
	counts <- tabulate(windows[i, ], nbins = length(habitat.labels))
	most.common <- which(counts == max(counts))

	if(length(most.common) == 1L)
		smoothed.codes[i] <- most.common
}

# Back in quadrat order, even when the raster has a different cell order.
habitats.smoothed <- habitat.labels[smoothed.codes[quadrat.cells]]
names(habitats.smoothed) <- quadrats$quadrat_id
c(changed.quadrats = sum(habitats.smoothed != habitats.original),
	total.quadrats = length(habitats.original))

original.map <- habitat.grid
smoothed.map <- habitat.grid
terra::values(smoothed.map) <- smoothed.codes
levels(original.map) <- habitat.key
levels(smoothed.map) <- habitat.key

old.par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
terra::plot(original.map, main = "Original map", all_levels = TRUE)
terra::plot(smoothed.map, main = "After one 3 × 3 filter", all_levels = TRUE)
par(old.par)

# Switch the map for the rest of the tutorial using the option above.
habitat.raster <- original.map

if(use.smoothed.map)
{
	habitats <- habitats.smoothed
	habitat.raster <- smoothed.map
}
```

Check how much area each habitat covers and which conditions it
represents. The table gives class sizes and medians for selected terrain
variables and Mehlich-3 phosphorus and calcium (mg/kg).

```{r}
#| label: habitat-environmental-profiles

profile.columns = c("elevation_m", "slope_deg", "tpi_m", "soil_M3P", "soil_M3Ca")

profiles <- aggregate(environment[, profile.columns, drop = FALSE],
	by = list(habitat = habitats), FUN = median)

sizes <- table(habitats)
profiles$quadrats <- as.integer(sizes[as.character(profiles$habitat)])
profiles$area_ha <- profiles$quadrats * quadrat.size^2 / 10000

knitr::kable(profiles, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

# Indicator species {#sec-indicators}

An indicator species is common across quadrats of a habitat and
concentrated in that habitat. `indicspecies::strassoc()` describes both
properties with `IndVal.g`. It uses the mean abundance in each habitat
to measure concentration, so habitats can have different numbers of
quadrats. The score is the square root of the product of concentration
and the fraction of quadrats in the habitat where the species occurs (De
Cáceres and Legendre, 2009).

```{r}
#| label: indicator-species

minimum.indicator.abundance = 1L  # Individuals in the whole plot.
number.to.show = 3L               # Species to show per habitat.

keep <- colSums(composition) >= minimum.indicator.abundance
stopifnot(any(keep), identical(names(habitats), rownames(composition)))

groups <- factor(habitats)
indicator.values <- indicspecies::strassoc(composition[, keep, drop = FALSE],
	cluster = as.integer(groups), func = "IndVal.g")
colnames(indicator.values) <- levels(groups)

# Keep the full score matrix. Show the highest positive scores for each habitat.
top.indicators <- vector("list", ncol(indicator.values))

for(h in seq_len(ncol(indicator.values)))
{
	scores <- indicator.values[, h]
	best <- order(scores, decreasing = TRUE)
	best <- head(best[scores[best] > 0], number.to.show)

	top.indicators[[h]] <- data.frame(habitat = rep(colnames(indicator.values)[h], length(best)),
		species = rownames(indicator.values)[best], indicator = scores[best])
}

top.indicators <- do.call(rbind, top.indicators)
knitr::kable(top.indicators, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

Use the scores to describe each habitat, including habitats fitted with
these same species. An independent evaluation requires other
observations. `indicspecies::multipatt()` can also examine combinations
of habitats (De Cáceres et al., 2010).

# Species--habitat associations with torus translations {#sec-association}

Harms et al. (2001) moved the habitat map to assess species associations
at BCI. Here `translate_around_torus()` moves the trees together and
keeps the quadrats and their habitat labels fixed. Trees that cross one
edge of the rectangle enter from the opposite edge. Each shift keeps the
tree pattern intact on the wrapped plot.

## Set up an independent fixed-map analysis

Use the selected `habitats` vector, the aligned `composition` matrix and
the matching `quadrats` table. The original `individuals` table must
contain `x`, `y` and `species` for all eligible trees counted in the
matrix. Use the bounds of the full rectangular `plot.extent`, with a
habitat label for every quadrat.

Choose the map before assessing associations. If the same trees helped
fit or choose the map, use the labels as descriptions of those trees.
For an independent test, use data that played no part in choosing or
fitting the map.

To use a saved map in a separate script, load the objects saved under
[Store results](#sec-storage).

```{r}
#| label: restart-fixed-map-analysis
#| eval: false

path.to.fgeo2 = "/full/path/to/fgeo2"
map.file = "/full/path/to/habitat-map.rds"

map <- readRDS(map.file)
habitats <- map$habitats
composition <- map$composition
quadrats <- map$quadrats
individuals <- map$individuals
plot.extent <- map$plot.extent
```

## Check a small rectangle by hand

Put two 20 × 20 m quadrats side by side in a 40 × 20 m rectangle. Two
trees of species A are in the left quadrat at (5, 5) and (8, 15). Two
trees of species B are in the right quadrat at (25, 5) and (28, 15). A
shift of 20 m in x puts A in the right quadrat and B in the left. For
species A in the left habitat, the observed relative density is 2/2 = 1.
After the shift it is 0/2 = 0.

## Specify the statistic

Harms et al. (2001) and the legacy `tt_test()` use relative stem
density. For each species and habitat, divide the species count by the
total count of all species in that habitat. Here we count individuals
using one record per tree. The abundance cutoff selects the species to
report. All eligible trees contribute to the habitat totals.

`OBS` is the observed share and `EXP` holds the shares from 999 shifts,
each calculated using its own habitat total. The score `mean(EXP > OBS)`
is the fraction of shifted shares above the observed share. A habitat
needs at least one tree for the share to be defined.

```{r}
#| label: torus-options

nsim = 999L
torus.seed = 123L
minimum.abundance = 50L  # Minimum number of individuals of a species in the plot.
tail.cutoff = 0.025      # Proportion in each tail used to assign a label.

stopifnot(nsim >= 1L, nsim == floor(nsim), tail.cutoff > 0, tail.cutoff < 0.5)
source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "03_spatial/R/new/spatial-null-models.R"))
```

## Align the map, counts and points

Use the quadrat edges to assign trees after each shift. A tree on an
internal edge belongs to the quadrat to its right or above, as in the
data preparation.

```{r}
#| label: torus-align-inputs
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Align the grid and check that the coordinates reproduce the counts"

stopifnot(identical(rownames(composition), quadrats$quadrat_id),
	identical(names(habitats), quadrats$quadrat_id), !anyNA(habitats))

# Map each grid position to its row in the quadrat table.
x.edges <- sort(unique(c(quadrats$xmin, quadrats$xmax)))
y.edges <- sort(unique(c(quadrats$ymin, quadrats$ymax)))
nx <- length(x.edges) - 1L
ny <- length(y.edges) - 1L

qx <- match(quadrats$xmin, x.edges)
qy <- match(quadrats$ymin, y.edges)
grid.cells <- cbind(qy, qx)

stopifnot(nrow(quadrats) == nx * ny, !anyDuplicated(grid.cells),
	all(quadrats$xmax == x.edges[qx + 1L]),
	all(quadrats$ymax == y.edges[qy + 1L]),
	all(c(range(x.edges), range(y.edges)) == plot.extent))

grid.rows <- matrix(NA_integer_, nrow = ny, ncol = nx)
grid.rows[grid.cells] <- seq_len(nrow(quadrats))

# Check that the observed coordinates give the same quadrat counts.
coordinates <- as.matrix(individuals[, c("x", "y")])
species.index <- match(individuals$species, colnames(composition))

ix <- findInterval(coordinates[, 1], x.edges, rightmost.closed = TRUE)
iy <- findInterval(coordinates[, 2], y.edges, rightmost.closed = TRUE)
stopifnot(all(ix >= 1L & ix <= nx), all(iy >= 1L & iy <= ny), !anyNA(species.index))

quadrat.index <- grid.rows[cbind(iy, ix)]
count.index <- quadrat.index + (species.index - 1L) * nrow(quadrats)
point.counts <- matrix(tabulate(count.index, nbins = length(composition)),
	nrow = nrow(quadrats))

if(!all(point.counts == composition))
	stop("The coordinates and composition matrix give different quadrat counts.")

# Select the species to report.
focal.species <- colnames(composition)[colSums(composition) >= minimum.abundance]
stopifnot(length(focal.species) > 0)

groups <- factor(habitats)
habitat.index <- as.integer(groups)
counts.by.habitat <- rowsum(composition, habitat.index)
habitat.total <- rowSums(counts.by.habitat)

if(any(habitat.total == 0L))
	stop("Relative density is undefined for a habitat with no observed trees.")

# Divide each habitat row by its total across all species.
observed <- counts.by.habitat[, focal.species, drop = FALSE] / habitat.total
rownames(observed) <- levels(groups)

focal.index <- match(individuals$species, focal.species)
keep <- !is.na(focal.index)
focal.index <- focal.index[keep]
```

## Shift the trees

Generate all 999 shifts in one call. Each column of the two coordinate
matrices gives one shifted tree pattern. The matrices use about 3.8 GB
for this BCI example. Use each shift's habitat totals to calculate the
relative densities and store them by habitat, species and shift.

```{r}
#| label: torus-simulation

torus.mins <- plot.extent[c(1, 3)]
torus.maxs <- plot.extent[c(2, 4)]

set.seed(torus.seed)
shifted <- translate_around_torus(coordinates,
	mins = torus.mins, maxs = torus.maxs, nsim = nsim)

expected <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(dim(observed), nsim),
	dimnames = c(dimnames(observed), list(NULL)))

# Read each pair of coordinate columns and count trees by habitat.
for(b in seq_len(nsim))
{
	ix <- findInterval(shifted[[1]][, b], x.edges, rightmost.closed = TRUE)
	iy <- findInterval(shifted[[2]][, b], y.edges, rightmost.closed = TRUE)
	quadrat.index <- grid.rows[cbind(iy, ix)]
	shifted.habitat <- habitat.index[quadrat.index]

	habitat.total <- tabulate(shifted.habitat, nbins = nrow(observed))
	if(any(habitat.total == 0L))
		stop("Relative density is undefined for a shifted habitat with no trees.")

	# Each focal species has one set of slots, one slot per habitat.
	count.index <- shifted.habitat[keep] + (focal.index - 1L) * nrow(observed)
	focal.counts <- matrix(tabulate(count.index, nbins = length(observed)),
		nrow = nrow(observed))

	expected[, , b] <- focal.counts / habitat.total
}
```

## Summarize the associations

At the 2.5% tail cutoff, the association is positive if at least 97.5%
of the shifted shares are below the observed share. It is negative if at
least 97.5% are above. Otherwise it is neutral. Equal shares count
toward neither tail.

```{r}
#| label: torus-results

association <- expand.grid(habitat = rownames(observed), species = colnames(observed),
	KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

association$observed <- as.vector(observed)
association$proportion.above <- NA_real_
association$association <- "neutral"

for(i in seq_len(nrow(association)))
{
	obs.share <- association$observed[i]
	exp.shares <- expected[association$habitat[i], association$species[i], ]

	above <- mean(exp.shares > obs.share)
	below <- mean(exp.shares < obs.share)
	association$proportion.above[i] <- above

	if(below >= 1 - tail.cutoff)
		association$association[i] <- "positive"
	if(above >= 1 - tail.cutoff)
		association$association[i] <- "negative"
}

table(association$association)
```

These labels describe departure from the shifts for each pair. For a
community question involving many correlated species, use a null model
that captures their joint variation. Zambrano et al. (2022) used
simulations to set joint thresholds for two overlap metrics within each
species pair. They then compared how often each association type
occurred across the community with its expected frequency.

## Inspect two example null distributions

The vertical line shows the observed relative density. The histogram
shows the relative densities from the shifts for the same species and
habitat. Use the table to find the score and label for any pair.

```{r}
#| label: torus-null-diagnostics
#| fig-height: 3.5

example.species = "ouralu"  # Ouratea lucens in the BCI species table.
example.habitats = NULL     # Or select two labels, for example c("2", "4").

examples <- subset(association, species == example.species)
if(!is.null(example.habitats))
	examples <- subset(examples, habitat %in% example.habitats)

examples <- head(examples, 2L)
if(nrow(examples) == 0L)
	stop("Choose a species and habitat labels from the association table.")

knitr::kable(examples, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

old.par <- par(mfrow = c(1, nrow(examples)), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for(i in seq_len(nrow(examples)))
{
	exp.shares <- expected[examples$habitat[i], examples$species[i], ]
	obs.share <- examples$observed[i]

	hist(exp.shares, xlim = range(c(exp.shares, obs.share)), col = "grey85",
		main = paste(examples$species[i], "in habitat", examples$habitat[i]),
		xlab = "Relative density (proportion)")
	abline(v = obs.share, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
}

par(old.par)
```

# Store results {#sec-storage}

Save the selected map as a categorical `terra` raster. The GeoTIFF
stores integer codes and the key records the corresponding habitat
labels. Keep any GeoTIFF sidecars with the raster. Save the quadrat
labels and analysis inputs in an R file so you can reuse them without
refitting the map.

```{r}
#| label: store-habitat-map

output.dir = file.path(tempdir(), "fgeo2-habitats")
# output.dir = "/full/path/to/outputs"  # Use a permanent folder to keep the files.
overwrite = FALSE

dir.create(output.dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

terra::writeRaster(habitat.raster, file.path(output.dir, "habitat-map.tif"),
	datatype = "INT4S", overwrite = overwrite)
write.csv(habitat.key, file.path(output.dir, "habitat-key.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

map <- list(habitats = habitats, quadrats = quadrats, environment = environment,
	composition = composition, individuals = individuals, plot.extent = plot.extent)

saveRDS(map, file.path(output.dir, "habitat-map.rds"))
```

If you ran the indicator or torus analysis, save the results you need.
Keep `membership.fanny` or the region probabilities if you use those
methods. They have one row per quadrat and one column per habitat.

```{r}
#| label: store-associations

# Run the lines for the analyses you used.
write.csv(indicator.values, file.path(output.dir, "indicator-scores.csv"))
write.csv(association, file.path(output.dir, "species-habitat-associations.csv"),
	row.names = FALSE)

saveRDS(list(relative.density = expected, nsim = nsim,
	seed = torus.seed, tail.cutoff = tail.cutoff),
	file.path(output.dir, "torus-relative-density.rds"))
```
